newsitem.title: CROATIA: FEATURE - Croatian language changes to suit statehood.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Croatian language changes to suit statehood.

text.p: Many Croats can only guess the exact meaning of some words written or spoken by President Franjo Tudjman. But his phraseology has become something of a literary standard.
New words, often sounding weird or archaic, pop up on state-controlled television and in newspapers almost daily, with native speakers sometimes taken aback by the imagination of their inventors.
Partisans of this language reform claim to speak "pure" Croatian and revive many words from 19th century writers, the first to invest their language with national identity.

They raise their voice against classical borrowings, words of foreign -- namely English -- origin and particularly those adopted from Serbian, with which Croatian merged 80 years ago into the previously unknown Serbo-Croat.
Croats say that after multinational Yugoslavia was formed in 1918, their tongue was subordinated to Serbian and conscious efforts made to rid it of its distinctive features.

For centuries before World War One, Croats and Serbs lived in different empires. Their languages, belonging to the same south Slavonic family, borrowed heavily from their respective Austro-Hungarian and Turkish overlords.
ATTEMPTS TO REFORM LANGUAGE
Since Croatia gained independence from Serbian-led federal Yugoslavia in 1991, it has been trying to bring its language back to the roots.

Calling it "Serbo-Croat" is now a blasphemy, although some linguists maintain that they are one and the same, or have the same relationship as American and British English, or German and Swiss-German.
Many observers say the attempts to reform the language at all costs have more political than linguistic motives.
"There is a tendency to show Croatian and Serbian as two entirely different languages," Vladimir Anic, a prominent Croatian language professor, told Reuters.
Linguist Dubravko Skiljan was also critical. "For our politics, language is first and foremost a symbol. It's clear it is to function largely as the symbol of the nation."
TUDJMAN'S INFLUENCE

The influence of Tudjman, forerunner of the reform, is vital. The 74-year-old autocratic "Father of the Nation" who led Croatia's secession in 1991 has been criticised for exercising too much authority in all spheres of life.
The reform is also backed by his political proteges within or close to the ruling Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ).

In 1994, a prominent HDZ hawk proposed introducing a bill on language that would have prescribed the use of pure Croatian and banned foreign names of bars and restaurants, which are very common in Croatia. The idea never reached parliament.
But attempts to achieve national purity have penetrated other spheres of life.
Tudjman brands foreign foundations which grant scholarships to Croatian students as enemies of the state and has denounced some intellectuals for trying to "denationalise" Croatian culture.
The list includes several writers and a Zagreb drama school that sought "to make Croatian theatre more international".
Independent analysts say his purist crusade is motivated by a desire to have monolithic control over Croatian culture.
"This is symbolically transferred to the sphere of language -- just like anything else, it cannot be left as an autonomous sphere functioning alone," said commentator Davor Gjenero.
But Zorko Sojat, an information technology professor and ardent advocate of the reform, dismisses politics as the driving force behind the reformists.
"I am not fighting against Serbian. I am fighting for Croatian, to be allowed to speak pure Croatian," he said.
For him the use of foreign expressions is part of an imposed petit bourgeois mentality practised by half-educated people who believe they can understand old Greek or Latin.
Sojat, who boasts the invention of the Croatian word for "helicopter", admits he is often laughed at for trying to speak Croatian "purged of all traces of unnecessary foreign words".
He is not the only one to be mocked for purism.
"Tudjman has tried to invent a Croatian with non-existent words or phrases nobody has ever used," wrote a leading columnist in the independent weekly Nacional.
"(His writings)...reveal a rare pretentiousness of a self-educated linguist that in some aspects resembles the linguistic rope-dancing of the American comedian Jerry Lewis."
While much of the population is irritated or at best amused with some of the inventions or resurrections from the linguistic past, not all are opposed.
"Woe to the nation that is not taking care of its language," said engineer Josip Pancic.

"It is a fact that Croatian had been wiped away for years. Now we have to dig out those words and offer them to people," said his daughter Sandra, who teaches Italian. "Whether they'll accept them is irrelevant."
Anic says such a change of language is detrimental to the whole Croatian culture.
"Our language is not developing freely. We returned it to the past and it's now stuck there. It is being controlled and destroyed. It's a language understood only by censors."
